During the '''1992–93''' English football season, [[Chelsea F.C.]] competed in the inaugural season of the [[FA Premier League]].

The season was the club's 88th year in existence since their foundation in 1905. It was their 58th season within England's highest tier of football and their fourth season of their current top-flight spell following promotion at the end of the [[1988–89 in English football|1988–89 season]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.free-elements.com/England/Goals/CheL/CheL5.html|title = Chelsea}}</ref>

==Season summary==
Chelsea started the season well and stood second after 19 games, but went into freefall after that, going 12 matches without a win, a run that pulled Chelsea down to 12th,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.statto.com/football/teams/chelsea/1992-1993 |title=Chelsea 1992-1993 Home - statto.com |access-date=13 January 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111126110143/http://www.statto.com/football/teams/chelsea/1992-1993 |archive-date=26 November 2011 |url-status=live |df=dmy-all }}</ref> replacing hopes of a title challenge with relegation fears. Manager [[Ian Porterfield]] paid for the team's poor form by becoming the first manager to be sacked in the new Premier League on 15 February. He was replaced by [[David Webb (footballer)|David Webb]], the scorer of the Chelsea winner that won the [[1970 FA Cup Final]]. Webb managed to steer Chelsea to safety, but his contract was not renewed by the board. Instead, they appointed former Tottenham legend [[Glenn Hoddle]], who had just taken [[Swindon Town F.C.|Swindon Town]] to their first ever top-flight campaign, as player-manager.

The club ended the season with 56 points, having won 14, drawn 14 and lost 14 matches.  By finishing 11th of 22 clubs, it was Chelsea's first top-half finish since coming 5th in 1989–90. With 54 goals conceded, this was Chelsea's best defence in the top flight, a record broken next season as well.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://chelseafootballclub.net/historytable.htm |title=Archived copy |access-date=30 July 2011 |archive-date=16 December 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031216182913/http://www.chelseafootballclub.net/historytable.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Chelsea went out in the third round of the [[FA Cup]] this season, beaten 2–1 by [[Middlesbrough F.C.|Middlesbrough]] away at [[Ayresome Park]].

==Kit==
Chelsea retained the previous season's home kit,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Chelsea/Chelsea.htm|title = Chelsea - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> manufactured by [[Umbro]] and sponsored by [[Commodore International|Commodore]]. It featured a geometric pattern on the players' right shoulder, repeated on the left leg of the shorts, an Umbro trademark of the time also used by [[Everton F.C.|Everton]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Everton/Everton.htm|title = Everton - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> and [[Manchester United F.C.|Manchester United]]'s <ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Manchester_United/Manchester_United.htm|title = Manchester United - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> home shirts of the same time. For this season, Chelsea re-introduced white socks as first choice for the first time since [[1984–85 in English football|1984–85]]. White socks had been introduced by [[Tommy Docherty]] for Chelsea in 1965, to make Chelsea stand out among other clubs wearing blue shirts, white shorts and blue socks.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Chelsea/Chelsea.htm|title = Chelsea - Historical Football Kits}}</ref>

The away kit was based on football kits of the game's early days as part of a nostalgia craze following the [[1990 World Cup]].<ref>'True Colours' by John Devlin</ref> It was a white shirt with red pinstripes, red shorts and socks.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Chelsea/Chelsea-change-kits.html|title=Chelsea Change Kits - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> Its laces were also worn on the Umbro home kits of [[Aston Villa F.C.|Aston Villa]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Aston_Villa/Aston_Villa.htm|title = Aston Villa - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> and [[Sheffield United F.C.|Sheffield United]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Sheffield_United/Sheffield_United.htm|title = Sheffield United - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> The Chelsea lion badge was included in a blue shield; the kits for next season retained this style. The kit was the final one in which Chelsea wore a red garment, the colour having been a popular away kit throughout the 1970s and 1980s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Chelsea/Chelsea-change-kits.html|title=Chelsea Change Kits - Historical Football Kits}}</ref>

Chelsea wore a third kit of all-yellow with a blue collar and pattern on the front,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Chelsea/Chelsea-change-kits.html|title=Chelsea Change Kits - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> also worn by Everton.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://historicalkits.co.uk/Everton/Everton-change-kits.html|title=Everton Change Kits - Historical Football Kits}}</ref> The kit was from an Umbro range called [[FC Porto|Porto]].<ref>'True Colours' by John Devlin</ref>
